newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian cosmonauts enter Soyuz ship to come home.
newsitem.headline: Russian cosmonauts enter Soyuz ship to come home.

text.p: Two Russian cosmonauts returning to Earth after one of the toughest assignments in the history of manned space flight left the Mir space station on Thursday and boarded a Soyuz spacecraft.
"I hope that everything bad that we've had will leave with us," outgoing Mir commander Vasily Tsibliyev said. "We are leaving. See you on Earth," he told the remaining crew.
Tsibliyev's remarks were carried on a television screen at Mission Control outside Moscow.
Tsibliyev and flight engineeer Alexander Lazutkin embraced the remaining crew and waved for the cameras as they floated into the airlock between Mir and Soyuz.
A Mission Control operator said they had closed the hatches at 9.47 a.m. Moscow time (0547 GMT) and started checking they were airtight.
"Please report when you have done this," the operator said.
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin were scheduled to don spacesuits at 0643 GMT, undock at 0853 GMT and touch down at 1216 GMT in the desert of the former Soviet republic of Kazakhstan.

Along with NASA astronaut Michael Foale, who will stay aboard Mir till September, they have endured a series of major woes since they came aboard in February. The most serious was a June 25 collision between Mir and its resupply ship, the worst incident in Mir's history.
The station has run on partial power since then.
"Thank you for the job you've done. Happy landing," a Mission Control operator told them.
After the June collision Tsibliyev began suffering heart irregularities which doctors said were stress-related.
He was given medication that has since been discontinued, and was not taking special medicine for the return trip, a mission medical adviser said.
Over the past six months Tsibliyev, Lazutkin and Foale have also had to contend with a fire on board and a series of problems with their life support systems.
One of them pulled out a plug on a computer by mistake while trying to fix the power supply, sending Mir spinning wildly for more than a day.
The Russian cosmonauts replacing them, commander Anatoly Solovyov and engineer Pavel Vinogradov, together with Foale, will have to try to restart the main oxygen supply system.
The Russians are due to enter the airless Spektr module, punctured in the collision, on August 20 to try to reconnect cables leading to solar panels.
